questions.question_text:
The unit vector in the direction of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is $\frac{1}{25}(24\underset{\sim}{i}+7\underset{\sim}{j})$ and $|\underset{\sim}{a}|=100$.
Find $\underset{\sim}{a}$.

options.why: Left off the scale factor, treating the bracket alone as $\underset{\sim}{a}$.
Multiplied the bracket by $100$ without dividing by the $25$ in the unit vector.
Multiplied the bracket by the reciprocal scale factor $25/100=1/4$ instead of by $100/25=4$.

questions.question_text:
The vector $\underset{\sim}{v}=t\underset{\sim}{i}+35\underset{\sim}{j}$ has magnitude $37$, where $t<0$.
Find $\hat{\underset{\sim}{v}}$.

options.why: Took $t=-(37-35)=-2$, using subtraction instead of solving $t^{2}=37^{2}-35^{2}$.
Subtracted the magnitudes rather than their squares and also ignored the condition $t<0$.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a unit vector?

options.why: Checked that the components add to $1$ instead of that their squares add to $1$; this vector has magnitude $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
Recognised $\frac{3}{5}$ from the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle but used it for both components, giving magnitude $\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{5}$.
Chose components adding to $1$; their squares add to $\frac{5}{9}$, not $1$.

questions.solution_text:
$\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{3}{4}$
$=1$
The magnitude is $\sqrt{1}=1$, so $\frac{1}{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$ is a unit vector.

Find $\underset{\sim}{d}$.

options.why: Multiplied the bracket by $51$ without dividing by the $17$ in the supplied unit vector.
Multiplied the bracket by the reciprocal scale factor $17/51=1/3$ instead of by $51/17=3$.
Divided the bracket by the required magnitude $51$ instead of multiplying it by $51/17=3$.

questions.question_text: Which of these is a unit vector parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}$?

options.why: It is parallel but has magnitude $\sqrt{1.25}$, not $1$.
It is parallel but its magnitude is $\sqrt5$, so it is not a unit vector.
Its magnitude is $\sqrt{2}$, not $1$, and its direction is not parallel to $\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solution_text: The magnitude of $\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}$ is $\sqrt{6^2+3^2}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt5$. Dividing by this magnitude gives the unit vector $\dfrac1{3\sqrt5}\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}$.
